title: Art and music debates
hookLine: scholars differ on musical instruments, while nasheed and recitation flourish

lines: LEAVE THEM. THIS IS OUR FEAST.
cards: It's Eid in Medina, and in 'Aisha's house two girls are singing. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is lying down nearby, his face turned away. Then Abu Bakr walks in, 'Aisha's father, and he's shocked.

Musical instruments of Satan, he says, in the house of the Messenger of Allah? The Prophet turns toward him and says, in paraphrase: leave them, Abu Bakr. Every people has its feast day, and this is ours.
The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aisha herself.

teach.b: Here is where scholars differ. Al-Bukhari also records a saying, in a chapter on drinks, that some of the Prophet's community will one day treat as lawful silk, wine and musical instruments.
Some scholars read this as forbidding instruments, and allow only the voice, and perhaps a simple frame drum at weddings and on Eid.
Others question how that report reaches al-Bukhari, or read it as condemning a whole scene of drinking and excess rather than the instruments alone, and allow music whose words and setting are clean.

teach.h: TWO READINGS, BOTH IN GOOD FAITH.
teach.b: Both sides are reading the same collection carefully. Neither is careless about the faith. Now the voice.
Nasheed, songs sung with the voice alone, or with a drum, are sung at weddings, in school halls and in headphones. And there is recitation of the Qur'an.
In Pickthall's translation, the Prophet is told to "chant the Qur'an in measured cadence."

teach.h: A FLUTE OF THE FAMILY OF DAVID.
teach.b: Al-Bukhari keeps a report in which the Prophet hears Abu Musa reciting and tells him, in paraphrase, that he has been given a flute from among the flutes of the family of David.

teach.h: CHANT THE QUR'AN IN MEASURED CADENCE.
teach.b: The praise for a beautiful voice compares it to a musical instrument. So the debate about instruments goes on, held in good faith, and the voices keep rising.

how: Muslims hold different views on musical instruments: some avoid them and listen only to the voice or a frame drum, others enjoy music they consider clean in words and setting, and recitation of the Qur'an and nasheed are part of daily life for people holding either view.

games.q: it's Eid, and two girls are singing in the house. Abu Bakr walks in and objects. you're the Prophet. what do you say?
o: tell the girls to stop at once.
leave them, Abu Bakr; this is our feast.
send everyone out to the mosque.
games.why: he told Abu Bakr to leave them: every people has its feast day, and this is ours.

practice: Think of someone whose view on music differs from yours, stricter or looser, and picture them choosing as they do because they're trying to be careful with something they love; hold that for a few breaths without arguing.
If you like, let a voice you love play quietly in your memory, a recitation, a lullaby, a nasheed, a song from home. If you pray, give thanks for voices.

wordCard.voice: Art and music debates. Scholars differ over musical instruments, in good faith, while nasheed and the recited Qur'an keep voices rising. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a song or chant; today, songs sung with the voice alone or with a drum.

carryVoice: Your line: views differ, voices rise. That closes the questions of today, from science reading signs to the tongue with thumbs. Rest well.
